item.title: Fans confident in Dolphins direction as 2026 season begins
item.description: Miami Dolphins fans seem positive about the team, even if the year is expected to be rough.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins are expected to have a rough 2026 season as they reset their salary cap, roster, coaching staff, and front office in one year. Predictions for Miami range from 4 wins this year to not coming away with a single victory. It might be a tough year to be a Dolphins fan.

The latest FanDuel Sportsbook odds have the Dolphins’ win total between 3.5 wins (-135 over/+115 under) and 4.5 wins (+140 / -165).

The fans seem to understand the current situation, and the hope it may bring for the future. While the team and new head coach Jeff Hafley will look for wins, this season may be more about 2027 and beyond. Root for wins now, but understand the importance of resetting the team and the growing pains that will come from it.

Dolphins fan confidence

According to our SB Nation Reacts poll, fan confidence in the team has held steady from the start of the preseason to the start of the regular season. Just before the team faced the New Yok Giants as part of the preparations for the regular season, we asked how fans feel about the direction of the team. The results had 80 percent of the fans thinking Miami was headed in the right direction.

Fast forward to just over a month later and with the regular season opening against the Las Vegas Raiders looming, we asked the same question and received almost identical results. Our first confidence poll of the 2026 season came back with 79 percent of the fans thinking Miami is headed in the right direction.

Miami Dolphins 2026 Season Fan Confidence Results:

Preseason – 80%
Week 1 – 79%

AFC East fan confidence review

As we reach the start of the season, it is time to also take a look around the AFC East to get an idea of how the fans of the Dolphins’ division rivals are viewing their team.

The Buffalo Bills, who are the favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, according to FanDuel Sportsbook, have an 85 percent positive fan rating.

The New England Patriots, coming off a Super Bowl appearance last year, received a positive vote from 96 percent of their fans. The Patriots have already fallen to 0-1, losing to the Seattle Seahawks in a Super Bowl rematch to open the 2026 season on Wednesday. Will that impact their fan confidence heading into next week?

The New York Jets, who finished last season with a 3-14 record and were in last place in the AFC East, have 63 percent of their fans thinking the team is headed in the right direction.

Just as a note, the range of fan confidence polls from across the league ranges from 98 percent of the fans of the reigning Super Bowl champions, the Seattle Seahawks, believing the team is headed in the right direction, to an even 50/50 split among Indianapolis Colts fans thinking they are headed in the right direction this year.

Do you agree with the Dolphins’ fan confidence poll results? Let us know in the comments.

item.title: 2026 NFL predictions: Super Bowl 61 opponents, winner
item.description: Our predictions for the two teams in Super Bowl 61 for the 2026 NFL season—and who will win it all.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 of the NFL’s 2026 season is upon us, and all 32 teams are still holding hope that this could be their special year. Us in Detroit have been holding that hope longer than almost anyone, but it no longer feels like a distant dream. The Detroit Lions have been in the Super Bowl conversation for four years running, which is more than the previous six decades combined.

But will this finally be the year that we can use the words “Detroit Lions” and “Super Bowl” in a sentence that doesn’t involve the words “never,” “missed,” or “crazy”?

Here are our staff’s predictions for Super Bowl 61:

Previous 2026 Detroit Lions predictions:

  • Offensive MVP predictions
  • Defensive MVP predictions
  • Breakout Player of the Year
  • Rookie of the Year
  • NFC North winner, Lions’ 2026 regular season record

Who will win Super Bowl 61 for the 2026 NFL season?

Morgan Cannon: Lions over Bills

After the Lions narrowly take care of business against the Los Angeles Rams in the NFC Championship game, they meet another team that is on the search for their first Lombardi trophy in franchise history: the Buffalo Bills. And after a back-and-forth game where there are plenty of fireworks between the two high-powered offenses, the Lions emerge victorious in a 38-31 win over the Bills. 

The championship parade down Woodward becomes the stuff of legend, and Detroit finally gets to celebrate the way they deserve to.

Al Karsten: Lions over Texans

The Detroit Lions will battle the Houston Texans in Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium, just two weeks after the Lions beat the Rams in that very same stadium in the NFC Championship Game and after the Texans went through the Bills at their new Highmark Stadium.

It’ll be a grind-your-teeth-down, bare-knuckle fight for three quarters, with both defenses holding the advantage before the Lions’ offense finally breaks through and erupts for two fourth-quarter touchdowns. Detroit will capture its first Lombardi Trophy with a decisive 24-13 victory, while Jared Goff takes home Super Bowl MVP honors, narrowly edging out Aidan Hutchinson—who will have made a nest and raised a family while living in the Texans’ backfield for four quarters.

Brandon Knapp: Rams over Ravens

Feels like this is the first super team I’ve seen in the NFL, and it’s the Rams last shot before they have to take things apart to get back up. I believe Matthew Stafford, Aaron Donald, and Davante Adams all retire after this season, and the Rams are doing everything they can to send them out on top.

Anthony Balaj: Broncos over Lions

Sean Payton vs. Dan Campbell is the storyline. Broncos win by a field goal. 

Ryan Mathews: Bengals vs. Lions

The Super Bowl will be a contest between the Cincinnati Bengals and Detroit Lions. The winner will be the one who scores more points than the other team.

John Whiticar: Ravens over 49ers

The Rams and Seahawks are favorites to come out of the NFC, but I think the 49ers are a legitimate challenger too; they were surprisingly good for how snakebit they were last season. As for the AFC, I think the Ravens might finally get over the hump with a new head coach; I think their offense and defense could both be top five units. Give me the Ravens to win it all.

Erik Schlitt: Rams over Bills

I’m going to keep things chalk with my prediction this season (according to most gambling sites) and pick the Rams beating the Bills in the Super Bowl. I’m not as in love with the Rams as most NFL media is, but on paper right now, it’s hard to bet against them.

Jeremy Reisman: 49ers over Broncos

Full disclosure: I’m the only one who made their picks after the first few Week 1 games, so I’m a cheater and a phony. But to be fair, I’ve always been a pretty firm believer in the 49ers and Kyle Shanahan (and I picked them to beat the Rams). If they can get even just a smidge of injury luck this year (off to a bad start), they’ll be as good as anyone. For the second straight year, I’m taking the Broncos as the AFC Super Bowl contender, because they probably should’ve made it last year, and they’re arguably even better on paper this season.

item.title: 5 things to watch when the Cowboys play the Giants
item.description: What things are you going to be paying the most attention to tonight?
item.content:encoded:
The time has finally arrived. The Dallas Cowboys are going to play a regular-season football game, and what better way to kick off their 2026 season than opening things up with a familiar foe, the New York Giants. Starting the year with a nice road win is a great way to get things going, but it won’t be easy. These revamped Giants have upgraded their skill positions and upgraded their head coach, bringing in Super Bowl champion John Harbaugh from Baltimore.

There are many things to occupy our attention, but here are five things to watch when the Cowboys travel to MetLife Stadium on Sunday night.

1. Confusing Jaxson Dart

The Giants have a fearless, playmaking quarterback who has brought excitement back to Jersey with an impressive rookie résumé of big plays. Whether he’s dazzling with his arm or taking off and strutting his smash’em, crash’em rushing appeal, he somehow finds a way to get it done. When he’s in rhythm, he can be an efficient operator with quick decisions and well-placed intermediate throws. And if he doesn’t like what he sees, he’ll go off script and use the legs to extend plays and see what develops.

The hope is Dart won’t like what he sees after the ball is snapped. The second-year quarterback can be a little Jekyll-and-Hyde, with the Hyde part possibly coming out if he is forced off of his primary look.

Jeckyl: Dart led the league in big-time throws while under pressure (10.2%)

Hyde: He was bottom in the league in turnover-worthy plays (15)

Cowboys’ new defensive coordinator, Christian Parker, will face his first test subject as the team employs its new deceit defense, disguising their intentions and then rotating late. Dart is the perfect victim. The goal is to make him hold on to the ball too long, and when he tries to play hero, step in front of his receiver and make him pay. Snap your fingers, and the ball goes to Dallas.

2. Interior attack

The Cowboys’ defense was notoriously bad last season, but no NFC team allowed more rushing yards last year than the Giants. They surrendered 145 rushing yards per game. Making matters even worse is the team traded away their best interior defender in Dexter Lawrence who was shipped to Cincinnati right before the NFL draft. New York will once again face challenges in the interior of their defense.

Fortunately for them, they’ll avoid having to face one of the best guards in the league, as we recently learned that the Cowboys would be without Tyler Smith for the first part of the season as he undergoes thumb surgery. In his place, Dallas will send out backup guard T.J. Bass.

Despite Smith’s absence, the Cowboys will look to attack inside behind the power of Tyler Booker and Cooper Beebe. Look for running back Javonte Williams to follow his lead blocks and use a physical rushing attack to keep the Cowboys offense out of third-and-long situations. And that is important because of item number three.

3. Pressure from the edge

As bad as the Giants defense is inside, they are equally impressive on the edge. Veteran Brian Burns is an absolute force, and they also have some recent draft picks in Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux who can do some damage. This is a very dynamic trio of edge rushers.

If the Giants are to have success against the Cowboys on Sunday night, it will come in the form of putting Dak Prescott on the ground. Both tackle positions have always been an area of concern, with left tackle Tyler Guyton offering up mixed results while right tackle Terence Steele can be downright awful in pass protection. The Cowboys also have a mystery at swing tackle and no longer have the Tyler Smith “break glass in case of emergency” option available. There is a range of outcomes where this one could get a little messy.

If the Giants’ defensive coordinator can deploy some creative pressure packages, that could be the ticket to getting the Cowboys’ high-powered offense off the field.

4. New guy excitement

The Cowboys front office has spent the last year loading, uploading, and re-loading defensive talent to the point where they don’t even have enough numbers to go around, and they have to bribe players from the offensive side. Unlike the 2025 unit that started the season, this new-look group has Quinnen Williams, Caleb Downs, Rashan Gary, Von Miller, Jaylen Thompson, and Cobie Durant. And the list goes on.

If some of these new guys waste no time making their presence felt, it will do wonders in building excitement for this football team. Whether it’s a Miller sack, a pass breakup by Thompson or Durant, or, quite honestly, anything positive from the rookie Downs, seeing these new investments produce immediate dividends will set the tone for the season, where they can finally turn the page on what was a dreadful defense.

5. Breaking the Banks

The second season of the amazing wide receiving duo of CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens will be full of excitement. All eyes will be on a great matchup between Pickens and Giants cornerback Greg Newsome II, as these two are very familiar with each other from their time in the AFC North. It should be a physical battle with those two fighting for every contested pass.

Look for the Cowboys to turn to their other alpha, Lamb, and utilize his shiftiness to create separation and cause problems for the other Giants cornerback, Deonte Banks. If Klayton Adams moves him around and constantly forces help over the top, it opens the door for some unattended receivers flying down the seam. With so much attention given to the Cowboys’ top dogs, don’t be surprised if Ryan Flournoy or KaVontae Turpin come up with a huge play in this one.

item.title: Madden Simulation Week 1: Monday Night Football! We are so back!
item.description: Let’s see how the Week 1 Kansas City matchup against Denver plays out in Madden.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs are home under the lights at Arrowhead Stadium, taking on theDenver Broncos. Let’s see how the game plays out in Madden NFL 27.

STOP!

If you want to watch the simulation without spoilers, start this video — or if you can’t see it, click here.

First quarter

The Chiefs’ defense held strong on the Broncos’ opening drive as Denver went three-and-out. Chris Jones made it look easy, getting through the Broncos’ offensive line for a tackle for loss to help force the punt.

The absence of Josh Simmons paid dividends as Nik Bonitto was able to sack Mahomes, forcing the Chiefs to punt. Kenneth Walker’s first carry in a Chiefs uniform went for two yards.

End of first quarter: Broncos 0, Chiefs 0

Second quarter

J.K. Dobbins was able to pick up a first down on the first play of the quarter, getting the Broncos inside the Chiefs’ 10-yard line. One play later, Bo Nix connected with Troy Franklin on a hard flat route for a nine-yard touchdown to give the Broncos the lead.

Brashard Smith picked up 21 yards on a second-down run, putting the Chiefs inside Broncos territory for the first time of the game at the Broncos’ 38-yard line. Three plays later, the Chiefs faced a third-and-eight, and Broncos defensive tackle D.J. Jones sacked Mahomes, pushing the Chiefs outside of field-goal range and forcing them to punt on a promising drive.

Following the Chiefs’ punt, Nix threw three straight incompletions before Denver punted the ball back to Kansas City.

Bonitto sacked Mahomes for the second time of the game on third-and-six in Broncos territory, once again pushing the Chiefs out of field-goal range. The battle of field position continued.

The Broncos would punt it back to the Chiefs, and on the ensuing drive, Mahomes dotted up Xavier Worthy twice. The first reception got the Chiefs across midfield, while another with 16 seconds left got them to the Broncos’ 25-yard line. Mahomes would end up being sacked by Zach Allen as time ran out in the half.

End of second quarter: Broncos 7, Chiefs 0

Third quarter

Andy Reid dialed up more chances for Mahomes to throw the football, as two first-down passes to Worthy and one to Tyquan Thornton helped the Chiefs get across midfield. Then it was the Kenneth Walker show, as he ripped off a 15-yard run before breaking loose for a 29-yard touchdown to tie the game.

Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s name was called in the rotation, and he made the most of it, sacking Nix to force the Broncos to punt on their opening drive of the second half.

The Chiefs went three-and-out.

The Broncos went three-and-out.

On third-and-six from the Chiefs’ own 46-yard line, Mahomes rifled a pass down the middle of the field to Thornton, who took it to the 22-yard line. One play later, a handoff to Walker got the Chiefs to the one-yard line.

End of third quarter: Broncos 7, Chiefs 7

Fourth quarter

On second-and-goal, Mahomes found his favorite target, Travis Kelce, for the touchdown to give the Chiefs the lead.

The Broncos punted back to the Chiefs.

The Chiefs once again punted back to the Broncos.

The Broncos punted.

Mahomes was sacked for the fifth time of the game on third down, forcing the Chiefs to punt.

Nix, from the Broncos’ own 46-yard line, found a streaking Evan Engram, who somehow burned three Chiefs defenders before dropping a catch in the end zone.

End of the fourth quarter: Broncos 14, Chiefs 14

Overtime

The Chiefs’ defense forced the Broncos’ offense to go three-and-out and punt the ball back to Kansas City.

The Chiefs marched downfield, and the Mahomes-to-Worthy connection resulted in two first downs. Walker rushed to the Broncos ‘ 12-yard line. Tyquan Thornton was left wide open in the end zone, and Mahomes found him on a post route for the game-winning touchdown.

Final score: Chiefs 20, Broncos 14

  • Box Nix: 15 for 25, 157 passing yards, 2 touchdowns
  • Kenneth Walker: 15 rushing attempts, 102 rushing yards, 1 touchdown
  • J.K Dobbins: 11 rushing attempts, 24 rushing yards

  • Tyquan Thornton: 4 receptions, 70 yards
  • Travis Kelce: 3 receptions, 20 yards, 1 touchdown 
  • Troy Franklin: 5 receptions, 65 yards, 1 touchdown
  • Evan Engram: 4 receptions, 44 yards
  • Courtland Sutton: 2 receptions, 13 yards
  • Nik Bonitto: 3 sacks, 4 tackles for loss
  • Zach Allen: 2 sacks, 3 tackles for loss
  • Felix Anduike-Uzomah: 1 sack
  • Chris Jones: 6 tackles, 2 tackles for loss

item.title: Justin Herbert needs 180 passing yards to be fourth-fastest to 25,000
item.description: The quarterback whom Jim Harbaugh believes will be remembered as the greatest of all time has a chance to join the all-time greats on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The quarterback whom Jim Harbaugh believes will be remembered as the greatest of all time has a chance to join the all-time greats on Sunday.

With 180 passing yards, Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert will reach 25,000 yards for his career. It would make him the fourth-fastest quarterback in NFL history to get there, via NBC Sports research.

Herbert, if he does it, will have done it in 96 games. Patrick Mahomes got there in 83. Matthew Stafford crossed the 25K boundary in 90 games. And Dan Marino did it in 92.

It'll take much more than statistical achievements to earn "GOAT" status for Herbert. His first career playoff win, for example, would be a useful starting point.

Before that can happen, the Chargers have to qualify for the playoffs again. In a very competitive division and a conference featuring multiple wild-card contenders, it won't be easy. Between the Bills, Patriots, Bengals, Ravens, Steelers, Texans, Jaguars, Broncos, Chiefs, and Chargers, at least three will have their seasons end in Week 18.

item.title: Gameday column: Key figures in new chapter of Bills out to set a great first impression
item.description: First-impression opportunities away Joe Brady and Jim Leonhard
item.content:encoded:
First impressions matter.

At least to our psyches they do.

They don’t always foreshadow. But they’re often the basis of reputations.

Nine years ago, the Bills went bold — very bold — in the draft, trading up twice for the most polarizing quarterback prospect, Josh Allen. Even Brandon Beane probably couldn’t have imagined that day in April 2018 that his first selection as the Bills GM would work out as amazingly as it has for the organization.

And after nine years with the most successful head coach in franchise history since Marv Levy, the Bills went bold — very bold — again, severing ties with Sean McDermott the morning after his team authored another agonizing playoff defeat short of the Super Bowl.

Buffalo stayed in-house with its hire after McDermott, and Joe Brady takes the sidelines today with the head coach title for the first time in his career. The defensive coordinator, Jim Leonhard, will also hold his title, in the NFL, for the first time. In years past, different defensive coordinators always shouldered the brunt of postseason-exit criticism in Western New York. Leonhard was arguably the most sought after defensive mind in football, a former overachieving player with a vastly different philosophy — and scheme — than the previous defensive-minded head coach.

To trot out a first-time head coach and first-time NFL defensive coordinator to begin a season with Allen’s superpowers at their peak… again, bold from the Bills.

And for Brady and Leonhard, what an ideal place to start… in Houston, a locale that, outside of Arrowhead in January, haunted Buffalo’s past regime unlike any other. While undoubtedly a major challenge, it provides an excellent opportunity to make a dazzling first impression.

Of course, the Super Bowl can’t be won or lost in Week 1 in the NFL. We have to keep that in mind. It’s a long and arduous rollercoaster of a season. For every team.

But for the Bills and their fans they knew exactly what to expect each year of the McDermott era, and it was unquestionably a span when Buffalo had its most prosperous and stable regular seasons in 30 years.

And first impressions still take time to shake, even today when opinions morph swiftly in the social-media driven age of the sports world.

McDermott won his first game as Bills head coach and ended a 17-year playoff drought in his first season. Allen’s first win, which came in September, was as emphatic as it gets, still the only occurrence in NFL history a 17-point underdog ultimately won by double digits (Buffalo won 27-6 in Minnesota). It also featured Allen’s original trademark highlight, which made quite the first impression. And that’s an understatement.

Those first impressions made indelible impacts in Buffalo for McDermott and Allen.

And now, just like when McDermott began in Buffalo, and at the inception of the Allen era, none of us know where to set the expectation bar for this new chapter of the team’s modern golden era.

We need a first impression to direct us where to start as the Bills venture into a new frontier.

Does the unadulterated version of Brady’s scheme, armed with the biggest receiver acquisition since Stefon Diggs, elevate Buffalo’s already well-oiled offense to new heights? Is Leonhard’s attacking style defense precisely what the Bills have needed on that side of the ball?

I suspect boldness will be a recurring theme from those two because such on-field evidence exists from their past coaching experiences.

And while the previous regime certainly won its fair share of big games, being bold wasn’t something that could always be said about McDermott and Co., especially in key contests.

On paper, a bold head coach and bold defensive coordinator align perfectly with Allen, the NFL’s ultimate on-field personification of boldness.

Yet football games aren’t played on paper.

And the Bills have a significant test right out of the gate, on the road, to begin this new chapter. I’d bet too that the Texans, despite their unusual level of accomplishment to date against Allen and the Bills, understand the significance of the test in front of them today.

Because while it’d be sensible for Houston to believe it just needs to run it back against Buffalo, these Bills are out to make a damn good first impression.

item.title: Jim Harbaugh tries to extend Week 1 record to 7-0
item.description: When it comes to the first game of football season, Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh does indeed attack the day with an enthusiasm unknown to mankind.
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to the first game of football season, Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh does indeed attack the day with an enthusiasm unknown to mankind.

Except for someone named "Potsy."

Harbaugh has a 6-0 record in Week 1, from his four seasons in San Francisco and two in L.A. With a win on Sunday against the Cardinals, he'll be 7-0 in Week 1.

And that will put him one more Week 1 win away from tying the all-time record. Via NBC Sports research, George "Potsy" Clark had a record of 8-0-2 in Week 1, from 1931 to 1940.

Clark's run started with the Portsmouth Spartans, who became the Detroit Lions. In 1937 and 1938, he coached the Brooklyn Dodgers. In 1940, his last year as an NFL head coach, Clark returned to the Lions.

It would be a surprise if the Chargers don't win today. They host the Cardinals (who have lost nine straight Week 1 games), and the home team is a 9.5-point favorite.

item.title: Eagles News: “Jalen Hurts enters the arena as once again the most polarizing player in the league”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 9/13/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Here’s where I’m at with Jalen Hurts: I’m not worried about the bottom dropping out with him. It would be shocking if he had a 2020 Carson Wentz season. I tend to think he’ll respond well to the questions about his future outlook because he thrives when he’s doubted. But in the event that he doesn’t have a good year as the Eagles’ offense struggles, it’s impossible to think that the team will act like that’s no big deal. In that sense, then, there’s pressure for him to play well and secure his next contract extension.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Starting 11: Jalyx Hunt, Jalen Hurts & The Most Fascinating Eagles entering the 2026 season – PHLY Eagles

1) Jalen Hurts. Why did Hurts show us the beauty of that mustache if he wasn’t going to keep it? Better to have ‘stached and lost than never to have ‘stached at all? Tell that to our bandaged hearts. The perception that this is a “make or break” season for Hurts is met with understandable ridicule. This is the Super Bowl MVP we’re talking about. This is the best quarterback in franchise history. But Howie Roseman is beholden to no one. And while the Eagles have proven the constraints of the salary cap to be bendable, it’s true they are staring down the barrel of having or wanting to extend the likes of Cooper DeJean, Quinyon Mitchell, DeVonta Smith, Jalyx Hunt and/or Nolan Smith this offseason. Can you squeeze a $60 million quarterback in there too? Savvy media literates are right to note the degree to which the organization has at the very least been comfortable with the blame for the passing game’s struggles landing on Hurts. There is also a power dynamic at play in which the most powerful person in the organization might bristle at the prospect of Hurts eating into that power too much. Or maybe some people in the front office simply don’t think he’s good enough. If that all sounds like the piling of chips on the shoulder of a person who has made a living and a persona out of turning those chips into fuel, you’re right. After the most radical offseason change of his career, Hurts enters the arena as once again the most polarizing player in the league. Can he make this season undeniable?

6 NFL players with the most to prove in 2026 – SB Nation

No. 5: Jalen Hurts, QB — Philadelphia Eagles. I’m really in two minds about including Hurts here, because he’s a very odd case study. Hurts is neither as good as Eagles fans believe, nor is he as bad as 31 other fanbases think he is. Ultimately he’s an above-average QB who is exceptionally good at running Philly’s system, but he’s not elite in comparison with other QBs around the NFL. The “something to prove” factor comes from the weight of expectations. The Eagles are routinely a team that should be contending for Super Bowl appearances with the weight of their roster, so when they fall short it’s only going to raise questions about whose fault that is. One of these has been Hurts’ consistency in the playoffs, where he very often looks like a shadow of himself — and that talk was stoked by A.J. Brown being angered that he wasn’t getting the ball enough. In many ways Hurts has nothing to prove, but he also has everything to prove in 2026.

    Why Baker Mayfield’s contract means the QB market could burst – ESPN

    Is he over the Baker Line? For sure. Hurts has been to two Super Bowls and won one. He has a 3.67 touchdown-to-interception ratio in his 10 career playoff games, of which he has won six. You can point out all of the flaws you want, but there’s just no way an organization has the level of success the Eagles have had the past five years if the quarterback isn’t good. If Hurts were in a renegotiation now and demanded to make more than Mayfield, it would be hard to tell him he’s wrong. But this exercise assumes he’ll be in a renegotiation next spring, and there’s no way to know how that will go until we know how this season goes. If Hurts flourishes in the new offense and the Eagles win a ton of games, he’s likely to be in line for something in the $60-plus million range. If he flops and they miss the playoffs, it’s not out of the question to think the Eagles would look to make a change. (Remember how Hurts got the job in the first place, so soon after they had extended Carson Wentz.) If it’s something in the middle — offense starts slow, picks it up late and shows promise, etc. — then Hurts and the Eagles probably figure out some kind of Band-Aid solution that puts off the big decision until after 2027. Fair or not, it feels as if there’s a lot of pressure on Hurts this season to show once again that he belongs at the top of this market.

    Eagles vs. Commanders preview: 9 things to watch – BGN

    To me, this looks like a bad offensive line. Based on my correspondences with Hogs Haven this week, Commanders fans seem to think it can at least be a league average blocking unit. Let’s say they’re right. Is average good enough to stop this Eagles front?I have my doubts. Jalyx Hunt had an awesome training camp. He looks ready to make another big leap in his development. Hunt’s stellar summer overshadowed progress made by Nolan Smith, who is healthier than he was last season. A.J. Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie showed juice as rotational contributors. Jonathan Greenard will NOT play … but the Eagles shouldn’t even need him to be able to generate sufficient pressure from the edge. And then there’s the interior. Jalen Carter. Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo are all poised to have strong seasons. They should be able to generate disruption up the middle, both as pass rushers and run stoppers. This trio contributed to stifling Commanders top running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt (who was limited in practice this week, by the way) last year.

    10 Eagles predictions heading into the 2026 NFL season – PhillyVoice

    2) The passing game will be up and down all season. The Eagles’ new offense under Sean Mannion is predicated on timing and precision. Run plays must look like pass plays and vice versa. Routes must be run with correct pacing and tempo. And Hurts must adjust to often having his back to the defense while running under center play action. It’s tough enough to master the intricacies of this offense with everyone healthy, but when you add in that DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon missed most of training camp, it could all look pretty choppy for while. On the bright side, the offense will make several improvements from 2025 to 2026.

    Eli to IR – Iggles Blitz

    They didn’t fill his roster spot on Saturday. That could mean they will sign Zach Ertz on Monday. The Eagles have talked to Ertz and there seems to be interest from both sides. We’ll find out if that leads to a reunion. They would wait until Monday so that the contract isn’t guaranteed. You normally see multiple teams make moves after Week 1 for that very reason. Stowers isn’t off to the best start with his career. He has missed time due to injury and failed to impress when he did play. Some want to rip the Eagles for taking him in the second round. Some want to label him a bust. I get the frustration with how things have played out to this point. TE isn’t a strength for the Eagles and getting so little from a high pick is disappointing.

    Our annual look at the Eagles’ top-10 players under 25 years old – NBCSP

    6) Darius Cooper [turns 25 Nov. 22]: Along with DeVonta Smith, Cooper is one of only two WRs on the current team who was here last year, and along with Makai Lemon he’s one of only two who are younger than 25. Cooper only caught nine passes last year in limited action, but he’s been so good this summer that everybody in the organization believes he’d be able to contribute if called upon in high-leverage situations.

    The Biggest Game in Town: Inside the Eagles Media-Industrial Complex – PhillyMag

    That swarm is swarmier than ever before. These days, at least 30 media outlets in the Philadelphia region — many employing multiple reporters, pundits, and prognosticators — offer daily, or near-daily, coverage of the Eagles not just during the season, but 12 months per year. Those organizations range from legacy brands like the Inquirer, WIP, and NBC Sports Philadelphia to digital entities like The Athletic (owned by The New York Times), PHLY Sports (a two-year-old start-up), Inside the Birds (podcast-driven), and Eagles Now and The Philly Special Show (two of a growing number of YouTube channels focused on the Birds). The amount of content they’re creating — and flooding our phones with 24 hours a day — borders on the ridiculous. On this day alone, for instance, after watching the Eagles do a 90-minute workout, the members of the Eagles Media Ecosystem will generate at least 250 pieces of content — articles, Instagram reels, TV news reports, TikTok videos, YouTube shorts, podcasts, whatever you call things posted on BlueSky and Threads.

    Cowboys fans are very confident heading into 2026 season, even with injury – Blogging The Boys

    We have Cowboys fans right where we want them.

    We also asked you if you were confident in the direction of the Cowboys heading into the season. There seems to be plenty of optimism based on all the changes and additions the Cowboys made this offseason. But does the Cowboys fanbase really feel confident in what the team is doing? You betcha. 89% of fans feel confident the Cowboys are going in the right direction.

    Washington Commanders Roster Moves: Offensive lineman elevated from the practice squad – Hogs Haven

    JGJ is a former Eagle. The Commanders can’t really afford an in-game offensive line injury.

    The Washington Commanders are elevating C/G Julian Good-Jones from the practice squad for Sunday’s season opener against the Philadelphia Eagles. He had been the team’s No. 2 center at the start of training camp, but Nick Allegretti’s calf injury had him taking first-string reps with rookie Matt Gulbin behind him on the depth chart. The Commanders were a little light on the offensive line after releasing veteran OT D.J. Humphries this week.

    Three Giants project to be top 50 pass rushers – Big Blue View

    Quarterback is, easily, the most valuable position on an NFL field. I’ve gone so far as to consider it the foundational position in roster construction, as opposed to merely a “cornerstone” position. By the same token, pass rushers have risen in importance over the last couple years. The ability and traits to win one-on-one and directly disrupt the passer. And in that aspect, the 2026 New York Giants could be sitting on an embarrassment of riches. Seth Walder of ESPN released their projections for the Top 50 pass rushers in the NFL for 2026 this week. All three of the Giants’ edge defenders, Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Kayvon Thibodeaux, project to be among the 50 most productive pass rushers in the NFL.

    Vikings convert CB Isaiah Rodgers’s playing-time incentives into a signing bonus – PFT

    Nice little boost for the Super Bowl LIX champ!

    Cornerback Isaiah Rodgers had a solid 2025 season for the Vikings. The team has acknowledged it with a tweak to his contract. Via Jeremy Fowler of ESPN, the Vikings have converted $1.5 million in playing-time incentives for 2026 into a signing bonus. To earn that payment, he would have been required to participate in at least 85 percent of the defensive snaps in 2026.

    Bralen Trice and Nick Muse elevated – The Falcoholic

    Muse and Williams are former Eagles players.

    The Falcons elevated TE Nick Muse & EDGE Bralen Trice from the practice to the active roster for tomorrow. OT Cameron Williams, claimed off waivers after cutdown day, has been placed on IR.

item.title: Steelers open to Joey Porter Jr trade
item.description: Steelers are open to trading Joey Porter Jr.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers’ ongoing contract dispute with Joey Porter Jr. could be reaching a tipping point.

The former second-round pick is not expected to play in the season opener against the Atlanta Falcons. He did not partake in training camp and is still getting “ramped up,” as head coach Mike McCarthy has said.

With the season set to begin, though, time has seemingly run out to get an extension done in 2026. The Steelers don’t negotiate contracts during the season, meaning the Steelers would have to use the franchise tag on Porter in 2027 if they wanted to begin negotiations next year. It may not get to that point, though. According to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, the Steelers are open to trading Porter.

“The Steelers have been open to listening to offers for Porter,” Schefter and Rapoport report. “But there has not been notable interest at Pittsburgh’s asking price of a premium draft pick — possibly in the first round — and no serious trade talks have developed despite the Steelers’ willingness to deal him.”

The Steelers do have depth at the cornerback position, as Asante Samuel Jr had a terrific training camp and preseason. Should he show that he is capable of being the starter, it may make the Steelers more comfortable to seek out trade partners.

item.title: What has you pumped for the Broncos vs. Chiefs matchup on Monday Night Football?
item.description: Here are some of the reasons why I’m pumped for the Denver Broncos vs. Kansas City Chiefs primetime game on Monday Night Football.
item.content:encoded:
Broncos Country, we are just one sleep away from the Denver Broncos taking on the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday Night Football to start their 2026 season. It’s been a long offseason, but the rubber is about ready to hit the road. I’m an enjoyer of most all sports, but the National Football League just hits different.

I’m so glad football is back. There truly isn’t anything quite like it in the world of sports. With that being said, I thought I’d ask what as you pumped for the season opener? Feel free to let me know your thoughts in the comment section. Here are a few things I’m stoked for.

The debuts of Jaylen Waddle and Jonah Coleman on offense

The Broncos had their share of ups and downs on the offensive side of the ball in 2025. The aerial attack had issues early on in the year—similarly to 2024. Moreover, the run game slowed down immensely in the second stretch of the season when J.K Dobbins’ promising season came to a halt after a hip drop tackle.

Truth be told, there weren’t many games where Denver had both aspects firing on all cylinders. To defeat the Chiefs on Monday Night Football, Denver has to start off fast, and they need to be able to attack Steve Spagnuolo’s defense efficiently in both phases. This offseason, they made two additions to help elevate their offensive production to the next level.

The first was wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. A tried-and-true beater versus zone coverage, Waddle has a chance to make an immediate impact in the Broncos’ offense improving an aspect of their passing game they struggled with in ‘25. I’m hoping he can make an impact on Monday night—a long distance touchdown from Bo Nix on the road in Arrowhead would be a fabulous way to kick off his tenure with the team.

The second was Jonah Coleman. He’s the Broncos’ insurance policy for Dobbins this year. In my opinion, Coleman will greatly improve their red zone rushing attack and improve their efficiency in short yardage situations. I’m not sure what kind of role he will have in his regular season debut, but I’d like to see him get an opportunity to show his promise in key situations against the Chiefs.

These are the two offensive players I’m excited to watch perform the most. Their success and impact will be extremely important for the offense to reach new heights in ‘26.

The rise and impact of Eyioma Uwazurike on defense

For better or worse, the offseason and training camp comes with a lot of hype. Over the course of the summer, we had numerous reports of players who have impressed without camp. One constant in those conversations from both players and coaches was defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike.

Last season, he had the best outing of his career. On Monday Night Football, he will be a starter alongside Zach Allen and D.J. Jones on the defensive trenches for the Broncos. Uwazurike’s size and length are both imposing and enticing, and I’m very excited to see how he performs against a Chiefs’ offensive line which may wind up starting an undrafted rookie free agent at tackle.

Stopping Kenneth Walker III and Kansas City’s revamped rushing attack will be mission critical for Denver to earn a victory in primetime. The former Iowa State standout will need to perform well for that to happen. I expect them to run the ball a lot, especially with Patrick Mahomes coming off an ACL injury.

In ‘25, the Broncos had a Top 3 rushing defense with respect to yards allowed and yards per carry. With John Franklin-Myers’ departure, the rise of Uwazurike will be essential for the unit to be as successful combating the run this season. I’m hoping he can help set the tone and tenacious play for the defense up front. He has all the traits to do so and I’m a believer in what he can accomplish this season.

Extending the winning streak versus the Chiefs to four games

Let’s be honest. Battling the Chiefs has been an ongoing struggle for the Broncos for ages. Prior to the ’25 season, Denver had dropped seventeen of eighteen games to Kansas City. It’s always tough losing to division rivals, but losing that many (including sixteen straight) was one of the darkest chapters in franchise history.

Though coming off three victories in a row and fresh off their first AFC West crown in a decade, nothing has me more pumped than the prospect of Denver starting off the season 1-0 and extending their winning streak against the Chiefs to four games.

Despite their success last season, the Broncos knows they fell short of their ultimate goal. This year, it’s all about proving themselves again. Opening week is a blank slate for every team looking to embark on their gridiron journey for a Lombardi Trophy. For many, it’s an unrealistic fool’s errand—but for the Broncos—it’s a reality. Starting off the season with a big victory should give them a much-needed boost of confidence facing one of the toughest schedules of any team in the National Football League to start the year.

It’s time for the Broncos to show everyone who the top team in the AFC West is. They can do that with a victory in primetime against their longtime nemesis. Let’s go!

item.title: Panthers fan bullish for future, but not for Week 1

item.content:encoded:
This week we asked fans of the Carolina Panthers two simple questions:

  1. Are you confident the Panthers are headed in the right direction?
  2. Do you expect them to beat the Bears?

In short, these were questions about the short term and long term success of the team. It’s hard to look at the work that general manager Dan Morgan and head coach Dave Canales have done and say that this team isn’t improving. It’s a short stretch from there to saying that you expect things to keep improving in the future. So it’s not surprising that a whopping 80% of Panthers fans are confident the team is heading in the right direction.

It’s all hard to look at where the team today came from and say that you expect any sort of success in the near future. Even with last season’s admirable showing in the playoffs against the Los Angeles Rams, saying you expect the Panthers to beat the Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams led Chicago Bears seems like a stretch. Never mind that Johnson is a younger and more recent head coach hire than Canales and that Williams is a younger and less experienced player than Bryce Young. Do mind that the Panthers have yet to translate a hot December/January into an even mildly competent September.

That’s how you get only 45% of fans expecting the Panthers to win their first home opener in years. Plenty more probably think they could win, but expecting a positive result is a whole different ball game. We probably could have gotten a stronger result in favor of the Panthers if we asked people if they thought favoring the Bears -3 over the Panthers was overly generous towards Chicago. But that’s not what I’m interested in.

I’m interested in the difference between people thinking things are going to be alright eventually and expecting them to be good now. I’m curious to see the drop in confidence after a Panthers loss on Sunday through extremely familiar events in spite of these seemingly low expectations from fans. I guess we only have a few more hours to wait to see how this particular cookie crumbles.

item.content:encoded:
Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is unlikely to play today against the Falcons.

Porter, who is listed as questionable with a back injury, is unlikely to go, according to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport.

The same report says Porter could be traded, as he and the Steelers have still not come to terms on the new contract Porter is seeking. The Steelers have said they won't negotiate with Porter during the season.

Porter said during the week that if he didn't play, it would be because of both his back and because he still has some conditioning work he needs to do after sitting out training camp. He has not said that he will sit out games in protest of his contract status, although that's certainly an inference some will take if he doesn't play today.

Porter is heading into the final season of the four-year contract he signed as the Steelers' second-round draft pick in 2023. He's slated to make $3.9 million this year, and any team trading for him would need to be prepared to pay him a whole lot more than that.

item.title: Jaxson Dart holds Giants’ future in his hands, wants to do ‘something special’
item.description: Dart is set to make first Week 1 start of his NFL career on Sunday vs. Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
John Harbaugh is the biggest reason for the optimism around the New York Giants entering the 2026 season.

Jaxson Dart, though, holds the key to just how bright the Giants’ future might be.

This is something I said this week during an appearance on the ‘NFC East Mixtape’ podcast:

“Everything starts for the Giants with John Harbaugh. You guys know what the Giants have been for the last 12, 13 years. It hasn’t been pretty. It has mostly not been enjoyable. There are warts on John Harbaugh’s resume from Baltimore. We know that. But John Harbaugh brought credibility. He brought culture. He brought leadership. He brought professionalism and an idea for how to build a football team that this organization badly needed. So everything changes with John Harbaugh. Everything starts with John Harbaugh.

“It doesn’t go where the Giants want it to go unless Jaxson Dart is what they think he can be at some point in the future. So, it starts with with Harbaugh, but if they’re going to get where they want to be, it runs through Jaxson Dart.“

Dart’s potential is one of the reasons Harbaugh took the Giants job. In a fascinating sitdown with former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin, Harbaugh said Dart is “even more talented than I thought he was.”

“When you watch a player every day in practice, you get a sense of what he’s capable of doing. He can really throw it,” Harbaugh told Tomlin. “He really has a great pocket presence. He understands the pocket. He feels it. He also sees downfield. Then he can get out and move and he can make plays. He’s got a patience and poise about him.”

That doesn’t mean Dart, a second-year quarterback with 12 NFL starts on his resume, is where the Giants need him to be.

“He’s learning,” Harbaugh said. “Our coaches are doing a great job with him every single day. He’s got to find a way to be tight and refined like all the quarterbacks do. But you don’t want to take away. You never took it away from Ben [Roethlisberger] …

“… There’s times that they’ll just they’ll look at you and you’ll know. It’s like, “Hey, man, I trust you.” You go be you.”

‘Backyard football’ isn’t enough

In his annual quarterback rankings, Chris Simms of NBC Sports had Dart at No. 22. That is one spot ahead of Cam Ward of the Tennessee Titans, and one spot behind Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles.

In an exclusive interview with Big Blue View, Simms said his biggest long-term question about Dart is whether he will ever be an elite thrower of the football.

“Dart’s got unreal feel and instincts, right. And his ability to extend plays and play backyard football is really where he’s special, and really a part of his game that I did not see that coming from what I evaluated in college,” Simms said. “He’s a pretty good decision-maker.

“I like his arm. I’m just saying I don’t know if it’s elite. I’m not sure it’s an elite arm. It’s a real good arm.”

Simms said Dart “hits the throws that are there to be made.” Simms just isn’t certain the 23-year-old can make the special throws that separate some of the elite quarterbacks.

“Do I think he can make some of the high level throws that I would say the elite guys in the sport right now can make? Mahomes, Allen, Burrow, Lamar, Justin Herbert, Caleb Williams, Matthew Stafford,” Simms said. “Those guys make five or six throws a game where I go, no, you don’t understand there. Nobody in football made those five or six throws today. That was a special play or throw or the ability to kind of slide in the pocket and throw a 25-yard laser on the right sideline into a window where, a lot of quarterbacks, you go, well, don’t even throw that. Don’t even do that.

“That’s just one area I think that I’d like to see a little bit more of, and be proven that he can do that on a consistent basis. And I guess I just haven’t seen that yet.”

Benefits of playing under center

Dart will be asked to play under center much more this season than he did as a rookie. The offense will emphasize play-action throws from the pocket. Dart wasn’t asked to do that often last season, and wasn’t great at it when it was required. Dart completed just 57.3% of play-action passes in 2025, 24th of 26 qualifying quarterbacks, per Pro Football Focus.

Early in training camp, Dart said the Giants had “repped the hell out of” under center, play-action. It is something we continued to see him spend a large amount of time working on during each practice throughout the summer.

Perhaps the under center work is part of helping Dart become “tight and refined” as a quarterback.

“I don’t know how much he’s done it [under center], but he looks good doing it. It hasn’t been an issue at all,” Harbaugh said. “I would say, under center in the passing game, it does really discipline your footwork because the drops are so important under center. I think it enhances – he would tell you it helps even in the gun, in the pistol, or whatever. It’s just another element.”

Simms believes playing under center, with the increased respect defenses have to give the run game and play-action, will be good for Dart.

“The greatest thing is it’s the best way to create explosive plays on the field right now is play action pass,” Simms said. “We’re at an era where it’s very weird, where explosive plays are actually probably at this point, more indicative of who’s going to win the game rather than turnover margin.

“So that’s again, where those big throws that we talk about and all that, I think they have more value now in the NFL than ever before, because the defenses are just so good. They’re so talented. It’s too hard to say, Oh yeah, we’re going to drive 12 plays, 75 yards all game long. There’s going to be a strip sack. There’s going to be a tip pass interception. So, you need to be able to make those explosive plays.”

Simms said Dart is “made for” the kind of offense the Giants are implementing. There is one caveat. Can he make the difficult throws from the pocket?

“Within that play action pass thing, I think we will get to [see] what you’re talking about, where, yeah, we’re going to see if he can make some of those big explosive plays into tight windows, because I think it’s going to be asked of him more this year than it was maybe last year,” Simms said.

‘Best quarterback in the world’

Jon Runyan Jr. spilled the beans regarding an interesting text Dart sent to his offensive linemen a few days ago, per the New York Post. It read:

“I want to be the best quarterback in the world.’’

Dart certainly isn’t that right now. He will probably never be. Simms has no issue with the goal.

“I have no problems with him telling his teammates and stuff like that,” Simms said “I respect the guy that puts himself out there like that and almost puts pressure on himself and expectations. He lets everybody know.

“Your great quarterbacks are all really wired that way … I do respect that confidence and a little bit of the burden of, hey, look, I’m trying to be something special here. So I hope that makes guys want to be a part of that.”

It’s no surprise that Simms said Dart won’t get there unless he does a better job protecting himself.

“The first thing is you can’t be in the top 10 [among quarterbacks] if you’re hurt every other week,” Simms said. “So let’s just start there.

“As you know, the best ability is availability. So, we can’t be taking some of these hits. He’s got to realize that the extra three yards are not worth what his value is to the team. That’s part of being the unselfish quarterback. That’s what you got to do.”

Simms believes the talent is there for Dart to be a top 10 quarterback.

“I really think he’s got everything,” Simms said. “I just want to see a few more of those in the pocket game-changing difference type of throws.”

Sunday’s will be Dart’s first NFL season-opening start.

“I think that I’ve just been waiting for this,” Dart said. “I think this is just the coolest stage, the coolest opportunity to play in front of our fans, Sunday night football against a team like the Cowboys and go out there and compete and it’s going to be an electric atmosphere and I can’t wait to be a part of it.”

Dart feels like a better player than he was as a rookie.

“I feel like I’m not even the same person at all. Obviously, the growth that you make from the experiences that you have from one year to the next. And I just feel like I’ve grown a ton through this offseason,” he said. “So, I feel comfortable. I feel like I’m seeing things really well. And this is going to be a really good test for our team and with a team like the Cowboys are going to be really competitive.”

There is a long way to go, though, for Dart to be what he wants to be. And what the Giants need him to be. Dart has been willing to put in the work.

“I think anytime that you are really pushing yourself to your limits on end, I think that’s where and really in any profession, whatever you’re doing, you’re going to grow the most,” Dart said. “That was an emphasis that I really wanted to put on myself coming into year two. Having a different situation than last, where this year I was the guy and I want to take the necessary steps to go out there. And I think that there’s a ton of extra motivation from this past season. And I want to do something special.”

“So, whatever it takes, that’s the same that we say in the locker room all the time. So, it doesn’t matter the time that you got to put in, whatever it takes to win and whatever it takes for you to be ultimately your best is required day in and day out.”

The quarterback position will always rank near the top of the food chain, and with Washington, that certainly is the truth, as Jayden Daniels remains the player the Commanders can trust most to make the offense function.

Head coach Dan Quinn has been beaming over Daniels since the microphone came on and he was asked a question post-draft about his command and accuracy. The biggest takeaway this year is that Daniels, while he didn’t play much in the preseason, had more than 500 reps in camp, including two joint practice sessions (with Miami and Baltimore). New offensive coordinator David Blough, while keeping the offense as secret as possible, has gone on and on about Daniels getting greater control of protections and operating from the huddle.

While the room feels much deeper this season, Terry McLaurin is still the top receiver, although Stefon Diggs would make that argument interesting. Mix in rookie Antonio Williams and tight end Chig Okonkwo and the team should have multiple options for Daniels to excel with.

What moves the ranking:

Whether this ranking increases or decreases depends on several things this week against Philadelphia, including how Daniels plays in the new system, how well he does with more control and more time under center. Does he operate within the system, looking for the open man and getting rid of it when it’s the best option, or does he try to play hero ball the second the play breaks down? He’s ready to prove to the world that he’s elite at the position, but there are a couple of last steps before he’s there.

Question: “You spoke about wanting to kind of keep the offense on edge a little bit, making them react to you guys as a defense. How does disguising coverages and making it look like one thing before the snap when it’s actually another thing after the snap help you guys toward that effort?”

And so how much of that, or how little of that do we see, that’s all depending on our personnel and how the guys feel comfortable. You know, the early part of the season, especially in a new scheme, guys want to just make sure, ‘I’m where I need to be,’ and that’s totally all right as long as they’re playing comfortable and fast.”

Question: “You have a rookie wide receiver making his NFL debut on Sunday, Antonio Williams. Curious in terms of what you’ve seen in his progression over this past month that makes you believe he’s ready for this moment, and what type of factor can he be on Sunday?”

“Yeah, a lot of growth. I think since the first day we’ve had him, he has been a joy to work with, and you see kind of the eagerness to learn. And then as we’ve progressed throughout, him earning rep share, different things over the course of the time, he has not flinched in any moment. So, you know, similar to a lot of guys on our offense, he’s made for kind of those big-time moments, and we knew that when we were evaluating him. He has confirmed that hunch since being here. So we’re excited about him and his growth, and we’ll see where it goes.”

Frankie Luvu can expose Jalen Hurts to the full force of Commanders’ defense

Jones will run something similar to what he learned from Brian Flores with the Minnesota Vikings. That will mean a lot of sophisticated blitzing and disguised coverages.

So many moving parts will demand quick thinking and adjustments from Luvu. He’ll be the voice of experience in the huddle, the player who rearranges alignments and switches in and out of play calls to keep the Commanders primed to execute Jones’ mix of pressure and deception.

This new approach relies on creating confusion for offenses. It’s a more thoughtful brand of defense than the reckless abandon Luvu often played with during his first two seasons as a member of the Commanders.

Getting everybody lined up, shifting would-be blitzing defenders in and out of gaps, and resetting coverage will test Luvu’s mastery of the playbook. The Commanders are going to rely on the greater level of comfort Luvu has compared to top rookie Sonny Styles.

The Biggest Game in Town: Inside the Eagles Media-Industrial Complex

For the Eagles, the microscopic coverage is the definition of a mixed blessing. On one hand, what organization or business wouldn’t want such sustained attention? Can you imagine someone writing an article about your product every single day for seven consecutive years? The financial value of the media exposure is incalculable — and one reason the Eagles are now worth $10.3 billion, the seventh-most valuable sports franchise in the world.

On the other hand, the year-round stream of articles, podcasts, and social posts has clearly contributed to what is now, at least in my opinion, an unhealthy mania around the Eagles — with every errant practice throw by the fourth-string quarterback setting off panic, and expectations for every season so high that nothing less than a Super Bowl victory will suffice. It’s a mania, I should add, that’s built to feed on itself: Fan interest leads to media scrutiny, which leads to deeper fan interest, which leads to even more scrutiny, which leads to even more obsessive fan interest, which leads to …

Take the case of Kevin Patullo, the assistant coach who last year was put in charge of the Eagles offense. When that unit, which was playing with significant injuries on the line, got off to a slow start, there were instant calls for Patullo to be fired. By November, the attitude about him had become so hostile that knuckleheads egged his house in South Jersey. The incident was covered by local TV, including 6ABC, which ended its report by interviewing an Eagles supporter outside a convenience store. The fan agreed that egging someone’s house was over the line, though he added that Patullo stank at his job — and should be fired.

Can you imagine any other circumstance when a TV station would cover a crime — then let someone say the crime victim should lose his job?

Perhaps that’s why the Eagles have grown more restrictive when it comes to player access. The chances of something innocuous being blown out of proportion are higher than ever. “They basically play defense now,” one media member says of the team. “It’s all about, how can this hurt us?”
